quick: Caution; fluid retention may worsen edema
Caution; oral/high-dose linked to hepatic effects
summary: Testosterone is an androgen used as replacement therapy in men with confirmed hypogonadism (primary testicular failure or hypogonadotropic hypogonadism) and to induce puberty in selected boys with delayed puberty. Diagnosis must be confirmed by low morning serum testosterone on at least two days. Subcutaneous pellets are dosed 150-450 mg every 3-6 months (each pellet 75 mg); other formulations (gels, injections) exist. Key risks: polycythemia, prostate effects, cardiovascular concerns, and fetal virilization.
indications: Primary hypogonadism (congenital or acquired) - e.g., testicular failure, orchiectomy, cryptorchidism
Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (congenital or acquired) - LHRH/pituitary-hypothalamic deficiency
Stimulation of puberty in carefully selected males with clearly delayed puberty

dosage.d: 150 mg to 450 mg subcutaneously every 3 to 6 months
dosage.n: Each pellet = 75 mg; adjust to clinical response and testosterone levels

dosage.d: Lower initial doses, gradually increased as puberty progresses
dosage.n: Monitor skeletal/bone age; risk of premature epiphyseal closure

dosage.d: Titrate dose/interval to keep serum testosterone in the normal range

admin: Confirm hypogonadism: low morning serum testosterone on at least two separate days before starting
Pellets are implanted subcutaneously (usually gluteal/hip area) by a clinician using aseptic technique
Do not use in women or for age-related (late-onset) hypogonadism where benefit is unproven
Re-evaluate testosterone, hematocrit and prostate status before repeat dosing
Counsel on careful handling of topical formulations to avoid transfer to women/children (where applicable)
moa: Endogenous androgens drive growth and development of the male sex organs and maintenance of secondary sexual characteristics. Testosterone (and its active metabolite dihydrotestosterone) binds the androgen receptor to stimulate development of the prostate, seminal vesicles, penis and scrotum, male hair pattern, laryngeal/vocal changes, and body musculature/fat distribution; it promotes nitrogen retention and protein anabolism and drives the adolescent growth spurt with eventual epiphyseal closure.

absolute: Known or suspected carcinoma of the prostate
relative: Severe hepatic, renal or cardiac disease

preg: Contraindicated in pregnancy. Androgens cause virilization of the external genitalia of a female fetus (clitoromegaly, abnormal vaginal development, labial fusion), most likely with first-trimester exposure. Women who could become pregnant must not be exposed.
lact: Not indicated in women and contraindicated; testosterone is not used during breastfeeding.
renal: Use with caution. Androgens can cause sodium and fluid retention, which may worsen edema in renal disease.
hepatic: Use with caution. Oral 17-alpha-alkylated androgens (not bioidentical testosterone) and high-dose androgen use have been associated with cholestatic hepatitis, jaundice, peliosis hepatis and hepatic tumors; monitor liver function.

major: Anticoagulants (warfarin) - androgens can enhance the anticoagulant effect; monitor INR and adjust dose
moderate: Insulin / oral hypoglycemics - may reduce blood glucose and antidiabetic requirements
Corticosteroids / ACTH - additive fluid retention and edema
minor: Drugs affecting hepatic enzymes - may alter testosterone metabolism
interactions.food: No specific food interaction for parenteral/implant forms.
interactions.alcohol: No major specific interaction; moderate intake.
interactions.diagnostics: May decrease thyroxine-binding globulin and total T4; alters lipid panel, hematocrit and PSA; may affect clotting/glucose tests.

serious: Worsening of prostate disease / prostate cancer
Cardiovascular events (MI, stroke - signal in some populations)
Worsening sleep apnea or heart failure
rare: Pellet extrusion or infection at implant site
emergency: Signs of stroke or heart attack
Symptoms of pulmonary embolism / deep vein thrombosis

monitoring: Serum testosterone to confirm diagnosis and guide dosing
Hematocrit/hemoglobin at baseline and periodically (stop if elevated)
Prostate assessment (PSA, digital exam) in men over 40-50
Bone age in adolescents treated for delayed puberty
counsel: Report chest pain, shortness of breath, leg swelling/pain or sudden weakness
Report prolonged or frequent erections immediately
Regular blood tests are needed to monitor red cell count and prostate
Women and children should avoid skin contact with topical testosterone (where applicable)
Do not share or misuse for performance/bodybuilding - serious harms can result
pk: Restores testosterone over days; pellets provide sustained levels
Pellets: steady levels over weeks; varies by formulation
Free testosterone ~10-100 min; depot/pellet gives prolonged release
Store pellets at 25 C (77 F), excursions 15-30 C
pearls: Confirm true hypogonadism with two low morning testosterone levels before treating
Monitor hematocrit - secondary polycythemia is common and raises thrombotic risk
Contraindicated with prostate or male breast cancer; assess prostate before and during therapy
Controlled substance (anabolic steroid) - high abuse/diversion potential
missed: For scheduled depot/pellet or injection regimens, an overdue dose should be given as soon as practical and the schedule resumed; do not double up. For daily formulations (gel), apply the missed dose when remembered unless it is near the next dose.
overdose: No specific antidote. Excess androgen causes polycythemia, fluid retention and hepatic effects; a single very large parenteral overdose has variable effects. Manage supportively, monitor hematocrit, and remove implanted pellets if necessary.
